signals.title: Show HN: Lettercamp – open-source static blog framework
signals.description:
Hi HN,

I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com.

Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web.

Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent.

Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog.

I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more.

The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. signals.title: Show HN: Tokspur a 3x faster open source inference engine for Macs
signals.description:
While we were trying to solve a separate problem, we ended up on a bit of a side quest and built an inference engine.

We got ourselves some nice, shiny new Mac M5 Max 128GB machines while doing a lot of local LLM work for another project and ended up wanting to run some bigger models.

When we were running models for coding, we noticed a few improvements that we might be able to make around repetition between turns. After that, the whole thing got a little out of hand, and we ended up writing our own Metal engine with native multi-token prediction.

The runtime is open source under Apache 2.0. I'd love feedback on how we've put the engine together, especially from people working with Metal or local LLMs who have an M5 Max.

We've only tested this locally, so it would be great if anyone could give it a prod and help us work out whether we are going crazy or not.
